To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) the activation volume for dislocation emission is a function of the unstable stacking fault energy and (2) that the activation volume is a function of grain size.

the activation volumes for the high strain rate deformation of nanocrystalling metals are in the range 1 − 10 ×  b 3, where b is the magnitude of the Burgers vector of a perfect dislocation, and that the activation volume is a monotonic increasing function of grain size.

the activation volume for deformation of nanocrystalls is a function of grain size, that this function is a monotonic function, that it increases with increasing grain size, and that it is in the range of 3 −10 b 3.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and testing of a new class of models that seek to explain the observed low activation volumes and high rate sensitivity associated with the deformation of nanocrystalls metals.
developing a fundamental understanding of the mechanical behavior of materials with nanoscale microstructure.
the development of mechanistic models to explain the observed activation volumes in nanocrystallines and the observed strain rate sensitivity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
nanocrystallinity is a mechanism that is capable of producing a high strain rate sensitivity, but the precise mechanism by which this occurs is not fully resolved.
the activation volume in metals with nanoscale grains and/or twins is determined by the intrinsic stacking fault, the unstable stacking fault, and the twin nucleation stress.
nanocrystallinity and nanotwinnability can be used to rationalize the observed low activation volumes and high strain rate sensitivity in metals.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the models provide a reasonable explanation for the observed low values for the apparent activation volume in metals with nano-sized grains and twins, and the associated high strain rate sensitivity.
the models presented here are capable of rationalizing the low activation volumes and high strain rate sensitivities observed in nanocrystallines.
the models presented here provide an important step toward rationalizing the low activation volumes and high strain rate sensitivities observed in nanocrystallline metals and alloys.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the activation volumes associated with the deformation of nanocrystalling and twinned metals are small and that the deformation mechanisms are fundamentally different from the deformation of conventional metals.
the activation volume is a sensitive function of grain size and that this is the key to the high strain rate-sensitivity of nanocrystalls.

the activation volume associated a given deformation mode can vary widely depending on the details of the deformation mechanism, and the activation volume can also vary widely depending on grain size.
